scenes.tts: The first film followed inherited evidence to a surprising pair. Once evidence is scored, how does a branching tree turn it into a claim about relatives? The answer is not the nearest tip. It is the path back to a shared branch point.

scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's COLOR MAP exactly: whale BLUE, hippo GREEN, tuna GREY, inherited evidence TEAL, common ancestors and branch points GOLD. Begin on its final tree, filling most of the frame. Whale and hippo tips glow, while a misleading double arrow measures the short space between whale and tuna tips. Replace that arrow with two question-mark paths running toward the root.

scenes.visual: Hold the moving tree behind the title 'Read the Branch Point'. Transform the title underline into a gold node and two branches after two seconds.

scenes.tts: Begin with a trait table. Each row is an organism, and each column is one inherited feature. A present mark lights up in teal. When the same marks form a smaller group inside a larger group, the groups are nested. A tree can show that nesting.
scenes.caption: Begin with a trait table. Each row is an organism, and each column is one inherited feature. A present mark lights up in teal. When the same marks form a smaller group inside a larger group, the groups are nested. A tree can show that nesting.
scenes.visual: Transform the tree into a large schematic matrix with three animal icons as rows and three generic inherited features as columns. Use check marks, not spoken or displayed numbers. Teal checks illuminate by nested groups: all three, then whale and hippo, then whale alone. Curved brackets wrap each progressively smaller set and slide toward the tree area.
scenes.narration: Begin with a trait table. Each row is an organism, and each column is one inherited feature. A present mark lights up in teal. When the same marks form a smaller group inside a larger group, the groups are nested. A tree can show that nesting.

scenes.tts: A useful marker is a shared derived characteristic. It first appeared in one ancestor and passed to that ancestor's descendants. Move its mark from the table onto the matching branch. Every tip beyond that mark belongs to the marked group in this tree.
scenes.caption: A useful marker is a shared derived characteristic. It first appeared in one ancestor and passed to that ancestor's descendants. Move its mark from the table onto the matching branch. Every tip beyond that mark belongs to the marked group in this tree.
scenes.visual: Carry the nested brackets back into a growing tree. A TEAL trait tile labelled 'shared derived trait' travels from its matrix column onto the branch before the whale-hippo split. Teal light flows forward from that mark to both tips. Keep an outside tip grey and unlit. Mark the whole diagram 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: A useful marker is a shared derived characteristic. It first appeared in one ancestor and passed to that ancestor's descendants. Move its mark from the table onto the matching branch. Every tip beyond that mark belongs to the marked group in this tree.

scenes.tts: A branch point, also called a node, represents a common ancestral population. Start at two tips and trace both lines toward the root. Stop at the first node shared by both paths. A pair sharing a later node is more closely related in this tree. Trace shared derived traits to branch points to find the closest relatives.
scenes.caption: A branch point, also called a node, represents a common ancestral population. Start at two tips and trace both lines toward the root. Stop at the first node shared by both paths. A pair sharing a later node is more closely related in this tree. Trace shared derived traits to branch points to find the closest relatives.
scenes.visual: On the same large tree, send a BLUE tracer from whale and a GREEN tracer from hippo toward the root. They meet at a pulsing GOLD node labelled 'common ancestral population'. Then send a GREY tracer from tuna; it meets their path at an earlier gold node. Keep both nodes visible, then show the full rule once beside the traced paths.

A pair sharing a later node is more closely related in this tree. Trace shared derived traits to branch points to find the closest relatives.

scenes.tts: Now spin the whale and hippo branches around their shared node. The tips trade places. Did the relationship change, or did only the drawing move? Follow both paths before you decide.
scenes.caption: Now spin the whale and hippo branches around their shared node. The tips trade places. Did the relationship change, or did only the drawing move? Follow both paths before you decide.
scenes.visual: Rotate the BLUE whale and GREEN hippo branches smoothly around their fixed GOLD shared node. Their icons trade vertical positions while the node, inherited-trait mark and earlier tuna branch stay fixed. End with the question centred beside the still-gently-moving rotated tree.
scenes.narration: Now spin the whale and hippo branches around their shared node. The tips trade places. Did the relationship change, or did only the drawing move? Follow both paths before you decide.

scenes.visual: Keep the rotated tree and question visible. Blue and green tracers continue moving slowly from both tips to the same fixed gold node. Do not show an answer word during the pause.

scenes.tts: Only the drawing moved. Both paths still meet at the same node, so the relationship is unchanged. Tip order cannot decide relatedness. This tree also has no top or goal. Every living tip has continued changing since its ancestors split.
scenes.caption: Only the drawing moved. Both paths still meet at the same node, so the relationship is unchanged. Tip order cannot decide relatedness. This tree also has no top or goal. Every living tip has continued changing since its ancestors split.
scenes.visual: Remove the question. Lock both tracers onto the same GOLD node and stamp a small label 'same relationship'. Rotate the whole tree sideways and upside down while the topology stays fixed. Avoid arrows suggesting progress. Animate equal gentle pulses at every living tip to show continued change without implying equal rates.
scenes.narration: Only the drawing moved. Both paths still meet at the same node, so the relationship is unchanged. Tip order cannot decide relatedness. This tree also has no top or goal. Every living tip has continued changing since its ancestors split.

scenes.tts: Branch length needs a key. On a plain cladogram, a long line can be empty space for layout. It does not automatically mean more time or more change. Some trees add a scale for time or change. Read that scale before comparing lengths.

scenes.visual: Stretch one branch dramatically while keeping every node connected in the same order. Label the panel 'plain cladogram: length unscaled'. Then duplicate the tree beside it and add a clear horizontal key labelled 'time scale' without values. Show a ruler only under the scaled tree. Mark both trees 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: A tree can only use the organisms and evidence included. New fossils, sequences, or traits can test its branches. Different evidence may disagree, so scientists compare several lines and treat the tree as a supported model. Scientists can update that model when stronger evidence changes the supported branching order. The clean classroom table is a starting case, not every case.

scenes.visual: Place the current tree inside a frame labelled 'organisms and evidence included'. Outside it, fossil, sequence-strip and trait icons drift in. One icon adds a dotted alternative branch labelled 'test', never 'rejected'. Let several evidence paths converge on the solid tree while one remains uncertain. Keep uncertainty visible and do not overstate certainty.

scenes.tts: So do not read across the tips. Trace backward. Find the first node shared by both paths, then ask which shared derived trait marks that branch. Rotation changes the picture, and a scale can change what length means. The branching order carries the relationship.

The TEAL inherited-evidence mark brightens just before it. A small rotation icon and scale icon move to the edge, leaving the branching order central.
